headline: Kenya's Soil Doctors are Helping Farmers Grow Smarter
meta_description: A UN-backed initiative trains farmers as 'soil doctors' to test soil and use fertilizers wisely, transforming agriculture across Kenya's 45 counties.
summary_short: Kenyan farmers are learning to test their soil before planting, thanks to a digital mapping programme that's already collected 3,600 samples across the country.
body:
Agness Munialo used to watch her neighbours dump excessive fertilizers on their fields, hoping for bigger harvests. Today, as a trained "soil doctor" in Kakamega county, she knows better. The Soil Mapping for Resilient Agrifood Systems (SoilFER) programme has changed how thousands of Kenyan farmers think about their land—starting with understanding what their soil actually needs. More than 3,600 soil samples have been collected and mapped across 45 counties, feeding into a digital system that tells farmers exactly what nutrients their fields require. When farmers provide a soil sample, the results arrive directly on their mobile phones, removing guesswork from agricultural decisions.

What makes SoilFER distinctive is its focus on local knowledge transfer. Selected farmers receive training to diagnose and repair soil degradation, earning the title of "soil doctor" and then teaching their peers—multiplying the impact beyond what external experts alone could achieve. The programme, launched through a partnership between the UN Food and Agriculture Organization and Kenya's Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization with support from the United States and Japan, has also renovated three laboratories with advanced testing equipment. Kenya's Cabinet Secretary for Agriculture, Mutahi Kagwe, emphasised the wider vision: "Before thinking about what to plant or the fertilizer to use, think about soil testing."

The initiative is attracting young people too. Jackline Kioko, a KALRO intern, discovered that testing soil could transform decisions on her family's farm—a shift that speaks to agriculture's potential to engage Kenya's next generation. As the programme expands to six other countries including Ghana, Mozambique and Tunisia, Kenya's example shows how simple information, delivered to the right people at the right time, can build genuine agricultural resilience.
quick_facts: 3,600+ soil samples collected across 45 Kenyan counties
Trained 'soil doctors' teach peers sustainable farm practices
Results sent directly to farmers' mobile phones
Partnership between FAO, KALRO, US State Dept, and Japan
Expanding to Ghana, Guatemala, Honduras, Mozambique, Tunisia, Zambia
